analysis.one_liner: Shields gun makers and sellers from lawsuits over crimes committed with their products.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, never received a vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended, despite 98 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal to sue firearms manufacturers, distributors, dealers, importers, or their trade association for harms caused when someone criminally misuses a gun. Any such lawsuit already in court when the bill became law would be thrown out immediately. The only exception: cases against someone who knowingly handed a gun to a person later convicted of a violent or drug-trafficking crime involving that transfer.
analysis.who_benefits: Firearms manufacturers, distributors, dealers, importers, and their trade association gain a near-total shield from civil lawsuits over the criminal misuse of their products, including suits cities had already filed.

how_it_helps.text: Bars any new civil action in federal or state court against gun or ammunition makers, sellers, or trade associations for damages from criminal or unlawful misuse of a firearm.
Requires courts to immediately dismiss any such lawsuit already pending when the Act is enacted.
Leaves only a narrow exception: suits against a transferor convicted under federal law for knowingly transferring a firearm used in a crime of violence or drug trafficking.

analysis.who_pays: Victims of gun violence and the cities suing the industry lose their main legal tool for holding manufacturers and sellers accountable for negligent distribution, and pending lawsuits would be dismissed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun violence victims and suing cities

drawbacks.text: The bill would wipe out lawsuits already filed by municipalities against gun makers, ending those cases without any hearing on the merits.

The only exception is extremely narrow: it reaches only transfers where the transferor is convicted of knowingly handing a firearm to someone who then commits a violent or drug-trafficking crime, leaving negligent marketing or distribution practices beyond the reach of courts.

Gun-rights supporters' good-faith argument is that the targeted lawsuits sought to use the courts to regulate or bankrupt a lawful, heavily regulated industry whose products were not defective, and that defending these suits raised costs for lawful businesses and buyers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives a large, one-sided legal shield to the firearms industry. It protects lawful businesses from suits over third-party crimes, but it also forecloses the main remedy available to shooting victims and cities seeking to change how guns are marketed and distributed, and it dismisses pending cases outright. The narrow exception does little for victims whose harm stems from negligent sales practices rather than a knowing criminal transfer.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never came up for a vote, so it died when the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Barr introduced the Firearms Heritage Protection Act of 1999 in the House on March 9, 1999.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and no markup, hearing, or floor action followed.
It drew 98 cosponsors: 86 Republicans and 12 Democrats.
The bill would have barred new lawsuits against firearms makers and sellers for criminal misuse of their products and dismissed pending ones.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun violence victims, cities with pending lawsuits, and plaintiffs' attorneys kept their ability to sue firearms makers and sellers in state and federal court. The industry remained exposed to litigation that the bill was designed to end.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Victims and cities kept their right to sue

for.name: Rep. Bob Barr
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 27 original cosponsors.

for.name: National Rifle Association
for.what_they_did: Backed legislation shielding the firearms industry from civil liability suits.

against.name: Rep. Henry Hyde
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Gun violence prevention and victims' advocacy groups
against.role: Advocacy organizations opposed to industry liability shields
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation that would bar lawsuits over gun industry conduct.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Republican (86 of 222) with modest Democratic crossover (12 of 211); no floor vote was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Firearms manufacturers, distributors, dealers, and importers
industries.note: The bill gives the industry immunity from civil suits over criminal misuse of its products and dismisses the lawsuits cities had already filed. The industry's gain comes directly at the cost of victims' and cities' legal remedies.
Trade associations are explicitly named as protected defendants, shielding them from the industry-wide suits they were facing.
The bill eliminates the entire category of cases these attorneys could bring on behalf of shooting victims and municipalities.
